ambiguities.impact: A formalization must choose a dimension-indexing convention; excluding m = 0 is an additional applicability restriction unless justified as implicit in “m components.”
ambiguities.issue: The source does not formally quantify or type the component count m.

ambiguities.impact: A formalization may encode classical differentiability, pointwise derivative existence, or another solution notion; assumptions stronger than existence of the displayed derivatives narrow the source's stated scope.

ambiguities.evidence: E2 displays the equation at (x,t), E3 gives the domain ℝ × ℝ, and E7 records the absence of an explicit quantifier.
ambiguities.impact: The conventional reading is that the PDE holds throughout its domain, but a formal target restricted to a single point or a proper subdomain changes the assertion unless that restriction is represented as local evaluation.

ambiguities.evidence: The page-23 passage says A must satisfy properties discussed below, while E6 supplies the later definition.
ambiguities.impact: A target merely encoding the constant linear PDE need not assume the eigenstructure condition; a target claiming to encode a hyperbolic system must include it.

contract_plain_english: In one spatial dimension, an m-component unknown q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝ^m and a constant real m × m matrix A define the homogeneous first-order constant-coefficient linear system q_t(x,t) + A q_x(x,t) = 0, with subscripts denoting partial derivatives. [E1,E2,E3,E4,E5] The equation alone is not automatically hyperbolic: that designation additionally requires A to have real eigenvalues and m linearly independent corresponding eigenvectors. [E6] The cited statement supplies no initial data, boundary data, formal regularity class, or explicit point quantifier. [E7]

definitions_and_conventions: q_t and q_x mean the partial derivatives of q with respect to t and x. [E5]
The equation is homogeneous in the displayed sense that its right-hand side is zero. [E2]
The coefficient is constant because A is a fixed matrix rather than a function of x, t, or q. [E2,E4]
If the system is described as hyperbolic, the book's additional convention requires real eigenvalues and m linearly independent corresponding eigenvectors for A. [E6]
hypotheses: A is independent of x and t and has real entries. [E4]
At every point where the PDE is asserted, q has the partial derivatives q_t and q_x appearing in equation (1.1); the source states no stronger regularity class. [E2,E5,E7]
implicit_context: There is one spatial dimension, and the problem is time-dependent. [E1]
Equation (1.1) specifies a class of systems that q must satisfy; it is not a claim that every function q satisfies the displayed identity. [E2,E3]
Hyperbolicity is an additional property of a system of form (1.1), not a consequence of the displayed PDE form alone. [E2,E6]
No initial condition, boundary condition, or formal solution space is supplied in the cited passage. [E7]

details: The system is first order, homogeneous, linear, and constant-coefficient. [E2]
It contains one time derivative and one derivative in the single spatial variable. [E1,E2,E5]
Both q_t(x,t) and q_x(x,t) lie in ℝ^m, and A acts on q_x by m × m matrix-vector multiplication. [E2,E3,E4]
The zero on the right-hand side is consequently the zero vector in ℝ^m. [E2,E3,E4]
Calling the system hyperbolic requires the eigenstructure condition stated later in the chapter. [E6]
Reality of A alone does not supply the complete hyperbolicity condition for an m-component system. [E4,E6]

undebatable_constraints: The equation must retain the exact zero-right-hand-side form q_t(x,t) + A q_x(x,t) = 0. [E2]
q is an m-component real vector-valued function on the stated domain ℝ × ℝ. [E3]
A is a constant real m × m matrix, so the product A q_x is dimensionally an element of ℝ^m. [E3,E4]
The subscripts t and x denote partial, not ordinary or discrete, derivatives. [E5]
The setting has one spatial variable x and a time variable t. [E1,E2]
No variable coefficient A(x,t), nonlinear coefficient A(q), forcing term, initial condition, or boundary condition belongs to equation (1.1) as selected. [E2,E4,E7]
If hyperbolicity is asserted, A must have real eigenvalues and m linearly independent corresponding eigenvectors; equation (1.1) by itself does not establish this. [E6]
